subtopic: Facing an ethical breach at work
subtype: Approach: staying silent to protect the job [Pitfall]
passage:
Subject: Why I've been so quiet

Dear Vandana,

You asked last week why I've gone silent in the team chat. Here is the honest answer.

In February I saw a manager change dates on some quality reports. I told myself it wasn't my business. My home loan payment comes out of this salary on the fifth, and I could not afford a fight.

Now the same reports are being reviewed by the client and I have said nothing. The thing I noticed has grown, and every meeting I sit through feels heavier.

I don't know what to do. Can you tell me how to find the company's reporting route? I don't want to keep pretending.

Abhinav

qa.q: On what date does Abhinav's loan payment come out of the salary?
qa.a: It comes out on the fifth.

qa.q: How does Abhinav feel about staying silent?
qa.a: Abhinav feels weighed down and guilty, saying every meeting feels heavier and admitting not wanting to keep pretending.

qa.q: What could Abhinav do first to raise the concern properly?
qa.a: Abhinav could read the ethics policy, find the confidential reporting route and note down dated facts before reporting.

qa.q: How might Vandana have felt on receiving this email?
qa.a: Vandana probably felt concerned and honoured that Abhinav trusted Vandana enough to confide.

grounding: The email shows an employee who fears for a loan-backed salary, says nothing about altered reports, and finds the problem growing while silence weighs on conscience.

subtopic: Facing an ethical breach at work
subtype: Approach: staying silent to protect the job [Pitfall]
passage: Ritu, you asked why I've been so quiet since the audit news. I'll tell you, but don't be kind about it. Last year I saw our branch head pushing loans through without the income checks. More than once. I had my own home loan, Ma's rent, and a job I'd waited two years for. So I told myself, it's not my department, not my business, he knows more than me. I kept quiet. Then the audit came this month. Forty-two bad loans. Customers who can't pay are getting recovery calls. Two colleagues who did speak up earlier were brushed off because nobody backed them. I could have backed them. I'm Abhinav, the one who always talks about doing the right thing, and I said nothing when it counted. That's what's keeping me up.

qa.q: How many bad loans did the audit find?

qa.a: Abhinav feels guilty and ashamed, kept awake knowing Abhinav stayed silent when the colleagues who spoke up could have been backed.

qa.q: What other approach could Abhinav have taken while still protecting the job?
qa.a: Abhinav could have written dated notes and used a confidential reporting channel, or backed the colleagues' concern, instead of staying completely silent.

qa.q: How might the customers getting recovery calls be affected by the silence?
qa.a: They took loans they couldn't afford and now face stressful recovery calls, harm that earlier action might have limited.

grounding: It shows an employee who stays silent about loan irregularities to protect a salary tied to a home loan, then carries guilt when the problem grows.

subtopic: Facing an ethical breach at work
subtype: Approach: staying silent to protect the job [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Uma, and I worked two desks away from Harish at the medicine distributor. Last spring I noticed him staring at the expiry-date report for a long time, then closing it. Later I heard the warehouse manager on the phone, laughing about 'relabelling the old batches'. Harish heard it too; I saw his jaw go tight. He had just signed for a car loan, and his first salary slip was pinned to his cubicle wall like a trophy. He said nothing. At lunch he told me, 'Not my department.' By winter, a hospital complained, inspectors found relabelled stock, and every batch from our warehouse was recalled. The manager was suspended, and our whole team was questioned for weeks. Harish looked grey through all of it. I can't know what he felt. But he stopped pinning anything to his wall.

qa.q: What did Harish tell Uma at lunch?
What might Harish have been worried about when he said nothing?
qa.a: He was probably afraid of losing his job with a new car loan to pay, which made staying quiet feel safer.

qa.q: What else could Harish have done when he heard the call?
qa.a: He could have noted the date and what he heard and used the company's confidential reporting route, since relabelled medicine can harm patients.

qa.q: How might the hospital that complained see the distributor?
qa.a: The hospital would see a supplier it can no longer trust with patients' medicines, which hurts everyone at the company.

grounding: It shows a colleague watching an employee stay silent about relabelled stock to protect a loan-backed salary, until the problem grows and weighs on him.
